subject: nesting: conceptual and technical lavaan questions

messages.author: cf1bcefdbd38a662
messages.subject: nesting: conceptual and technical lavaan questions
parts:
Hi, 

I would appreciate conceptual and technical help thinking through an analysis. 

Conceptual

Let's say I have the following 5 models I want to test for a fake 9-item ordinal dataset (run the code below to plot with semPlot for visual diagrams):

A. 1 first-order factor (f0)
B. 3 first order correlated factors (f1, f2, f3)
C. 3 first order correlated factors (f1, f2, f3) with two cross-loading items on f1 and f2
D. hierarchical: 1 second-order factor (g), 3 first-order uncorrelated factors (f1, f2, f3)
E. bifactor: 1 general factor (g) and 3 first-order uncorrelated factors (f1, f2, f3)

I believe the nesting is as follows:
A within B (constrain factor correlations to get A)
B within C (constrain cross-loadings of C to get B)
D within B (second-order nested within first-order correlated factors models)
D within E (per Yung et al., 1999)
 
Question 1: Is the above nesting correct?
Question 2: Is D also nested with C? If D is within B, and B is within C, then I think D should also be within C.

Technical

Let's assume I am correct about the nesting and shift to programming. I created a reproducible example here that shows all five models. 

Question 3: Do the models look like they are specified correctly in lavaan? Any suggested improvements to the specifications to match the descriptions of each model?


Thanks for considering this request.

Eric

messages.author: 99a06696c483481a
messages.subject: Re: nesting: conceptual and technical lavaan questions
parts:
Models B and D are equivalent models.  DF and fit will be identical.  I haven't read the Yung paper, but I would have said that D and E are not nested because going from D to E involves relaxing some constraints (loadings of the observed variables directly on the broad factor) and constraining others (relations between the specific factors and the broad factor).
     Regarding your code, I'm not the expert, but recently someone reported some odd behavior when estimating an hierarchical model.  An alternative to your code was to specify a loading, fixed at 0, for the second order factor on some observed variable, and then just regress the first order factors on the second order factor.
--Ed Rigdon

mod.A <- "\n f0 =~ v1 + v2 + v3 + v4 + v5 + v6 + v7 + v8 + v9\n "

Perhaps this is due to copy/pasting, but the '\n' characters are not
needed in the model syntax. If you need more than 1 formula on the same
line, you can use ";" as in

mod.B <- 'f1 =~ v1 + v2 + v3; f2 =~ v4 + v5 + v6; f3 =~ v7 + v8 + v9'

Also note: single quotes for surrounding the model syntax are preferred.
EG: I neglected to add the chunk option tidy=FALSE, so knitr removed my line breaks, added /n, and converted to double quotes. I've updated the example.

As for Model D: the f1 ~~ 0*f2 + 0*f3\n f2 ~~ 0*f3\n are not needed,
since they are estimated by default (if g is a higher-order factor).

Yves.
EG: OK. Thanks. I updated my example.

A. 1 first-order factor (f0)
B. 3 first order correlated factors (f1, f2, f3)
C. 3 first order correlated factors (f1, f2, f3) with two cross-loading items on f1 and f2
D. hierarchical: 1 second-order factor (g), 3 first-order uncorrelated factors (f1, f2, f3)
E. bifactor: 1 general factor (g) and 3 first-order uncorrelated factors (f1, f2, f3)

I believe the nesting is as follows:
A within B (constrain factor correlations to get A)
B within C (constrain cross-loadings of C to get B)
D within B (second-order nested within first-order correlated factors models)
D within E (per Yung et al., 1999)
 
Question 1: Is the above nesting correct?
Question 2: Is D also nested with C? If D is within B, and B is within C, then I think D should also be within C.

Eric,

For some time, I have been meaning to write a function for the semTools package to implement tests for nesting and equivalence, using Bentler & Satorra's (2010) method (see attached PDF).  This motivates me to get it done soon.  Below is the "engine" for that function, which will test whether model "x" is nested within model "y" -- bearing in mind that model equivalence is a special case of nesting when the nested models have equal degrees of freedom (or equivalently, the same number of parameter estimates).  You can use this function to test your models, one pair at a time, for nesting/equivalence by passing your fitted lavaan objects to the model (e.g., fit.mod.A and fit.mod.B):

x.within.y <- function(x, y, crit = .0001) {
  require(lavaan)
  prepCov <- function(x, varNames) {
    for (g in seq_along(x)) {
      colnames(x[[g]]) <- varNames[[g]]
      rownames(x[[g]]) <- varNames[[g]]
    }
    x
  }
  prepMu <- function(x, varNames) {
    for (g in seq_along(x)) {
      x[[g]] <- as.numeric(x[[g]])
      names(x[[g]]) <- varNames[[g]]
    }
    x
  }
 
  ## check the data information matches (e.g., sample sizes)
  if (!identical(x@Data, y@Data)) stop("Models must apply to the same data")

  ## variable names
  if (identical(x@pta$vnames$ov, y@pta$vnames$ov)) {
    varNames <- x@pta$vnames$ov
  } else {
    stop("Models do not contain the same variables")
  }

  ## check degrees of freedom support nesting structure
  if (inspect(x, "fit")["df"] < inspect(y, "fit")["df"]) stop("
      x cannot be nested within y because y is more restricted than x")

  ## model-implied moments
  Sigma <- prepCov(x@Fi...@Sigma.hat, varNames)
  Mu <- prepMu(x@Fi...@Mu.hat, varNames)

  ## fit model and inspect chi-squared
  myFit <- lavaan(sample.cov = Sigma, sample.mean = Mu, sample.nobs = x@Data@nobs,
                  slotParTable = y@ParTable, slotModel = y@Model, slotOptions = y@Options)
  result <- inspect(myFit, "fit")["chisq"] < crit
  names(result) <- NULL
  if (inspect(x, "fit")["df"] == inspect(y, "fit")["df"]) return(c(Equivalent = result))
  c(Nested = result)
}

Also attached is an R script that includes this function and some examples to run, so you can see how it works.

Soon, I'll submit a more generic function to semTools that will accept any number of fitted lavaan objects, sort them according to the number of degrees of freedom, make the necessary tests, and return a logical matrix indicating the nesting/equivalence relationships.  I might make it general enough that you could simply pass model syntax as well, in which case the function would simulate data for the tests, as described in Bentler & Satorra (2010).  Watch this space :-)

Terry

Yves,

A user recently brought something to my attention that causes a problem with the nesting/equivalence testing function in semTools.  When using WLS estimator, net() returns an error that if the raw data is not provided, the WLS.V weight matrix must be provided along with the sample.cov/means/nobs.  But when I pass the WLS.V matrix, I still get an error that seems to regard the thresholds (which I don't think can be passed to the lavaan function like WLS.V can).

Could you suggest a solution, or let me know whether the net() help page should warn that the implementation does not work for WLS?  I provide example syntax below to reproduce the error that I can't figure a way to solve.  Thank you,

Terry

library(lavaan)

myData <- read.table("http://www.statmodel.com/usersguide/chap5/ex5.16.dat")
names(myData) <- c("u1","u2","u3","u4","u5","u6","x1","x2","x3","g")

## specify more restricted model
mod0 <- ' f1 =~ u1 + u2 + u3 + u4 + u5 + u6 '
## specify less restricted model
mod1 <- '
f1 =~ u1 + u2 + u3
f2 =~ u4 + u5 + u6
'
## fit both models to data
fit0 <- cfa(mod0, data = myData, ordered = paste0("u", 1:6))
fit1 <- cfa(mod1, data = myData, ordered = paste0("u", 1:6))

## extract more-restricted model-implied stats
R <- fit0@Fi...@Sigma.hat[[1]]
colnames(R) <- paste0("u", 1:6)
rownames(R) <- paste0("u", 1:6)
M <- as.numeric(fit0@Fi...@Mu.hat[[1]])
names(M) <- paste0("u", 1:6)

## fit less-restricted model to model-implied stats from more-restricted model
myFit <- lavaan(sample.cov = R, sample.mean = M, sample.nobs = nrow(myData),
                slotParTable = fit1@ParTable, slotOptions = fit1@Options,
                WLS.V = fit0@Sam...@WLS.V)
# inspect(myFit, "fit")["chisq"]

On 08/26/2014 07:45 AM, Terrence Jorgensen wrote:
> Could you suggest a solution, or let me know whether the net() help page
> should warn that the implementation does not work for WLS?

I had a look a this, and I am afraid there is no easy solution. It would
be fairly easy to provide a sample.th= argument, but that is not enough.
I also need a th.idx vector (for keeping track which thresholds belong
to which variable), and it is less trivial for a user to provide this in
a correct form. (I also would need th.nox and th.names).

For 0.5-17, I would suggest that you warn that this is not implemented.
For future versions, I need to think about possible solutions...

Yves.
